cards.title: 3.1.1 The Concept of Force
body: A spring balance, a 1 kg mass, a length of spring and a small box.
In physics, a force is a push or a pull exerted by one object on another.
When the wind blows the leaves of a tree, the wind exerts a force.
Forces are physical quantities that can be measured. using a force meter.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Newton’s First Law of Motion
body: When no forces are exerted on an object or when the vector sum of all the forces is zero, the net force is zero.
If an object moves with a constant velocity, then the net force on the object is zero.
The forward force must be equal in size and opposite in direction to the force of friction in order to maintain constant velocity.
If there is no friction, there is no need for a forward force.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Newton’s Second Law of Motion
body: Newton’s first law describes what happens when the net force acting on an object is zero.
In that case, the object either remains at rest or continues to move in a straight line at constant speed.
In other words, an unbalanced force, or net force, accelerates or decelerates.
Newton’s second law involves force, mass, and acceleration.

cards.title: 3.1.4 Newton’s Third Law of Motion
body: Newton’s first and second laws explain how the changes in the motion of a single object changes.
Newton stated that a force applied to one object always comes from another object.
For example, the force of gravity on a falling orange comes from the Earth and the magnetic force acting on a metal nail comes from a magnet.
In other words, one force cannot exist without the other.

cards.title: 3.1.5 Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation
body: One day Sir Isaac Newton was sitting in his garden and noticed an apple dropped from a tree.
The sight of the falling apple made him think about the problem of motion of the planets.
Newton realised that the force on the apple must be proportional to its mass.
**Gravitational force** is a property of all matter; that is, every object attracts every other object with a gravitational force.

cards.title: 3.1.6 Normal Force
body: The cupboard exerts a downward force on the floor.
According to Newton’s third law of motion, the floor exerts an upward force on the cupboard.
The force that is exerted by a supporting surface on an object that is resting (standing, sitting, lying) on it is called the **normal force**, FN.
**Normal force** is a contact force between two solid objects and acts that is perpendicularly to the contact surfaces (e.g. cupboard and floor).

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following is the standard SI unit of force?

steps.text: **Given:** Basic units of physical quantities.
**Formula:** The SI unit of force is the Newton ($$\text{N}$$, named after Sir Isaac Newton).
**Substitution:** Comparing options: Joule is for energy, Kilogram is for mass, Watt is for power, and Newton is for force.
**Final Result:** The correct option is **D. Newton**.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: An object is acted upon by two collinear forces: $$12\text{ N}$$ acting East and $$8\text{ N}$$ acting West. What is the net force acting on the object?

steps.text: **Given:** Force East $$F_1 = +12\text{ N}$$, Force West $$F_2 = -8\text{ N}$$.
**Formula:** $$F_{net} = F_1 + F_2$$
**Substitution:** $$F_{net} = +12\text{ N} + (-8\text{ N}) = +4\text{ N}$$ (which points East).
**Final Result:** The net force is **$$4\text{ N}$$ East**.

cards.why:
**Given:** Force East $$F_1 = +12\text{ N}$$, Force West $$F_2 = -8\text{ N}$$.

**Substitution:** $$F_{net} = +12\text{ N} + (-8\text{ N}) = +4\text{ N}$$ (which points East).

**Final Result:** The net force is **$$4\text{ N}$$ East**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the net unbalanced force acting on an object is zero, according to Newton's first law, the object must:

options.C: Maintain its constant velocity (or remain at rest)

cards.why:
**Given:** Net force $$F_{net} = 0$$.

**Formula:** From Newton's first law, if $$F_{net} = 0$$, then acceleration $$a = 0$$.

**Substitution:** Zero acceleration means the velocity of the object does not change over time. Thus, it remains at rest if initially at rest, or continues at a constant velocity.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **C. Maintain its constant velocity (or remain at rest)**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the distance between two masses is doubled, according to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the gravitational force between them:
cards.why:
**Given:** Initial distance $$r$$, final distance $$r' = 2r$$.

**Formula:** $$F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$

**Substitution:** $$F' = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{(2r)^2} = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{4r^2} = \frac{1}{4}F$$.

**Final Result:** The gravitational force becomes **one-fourth** of the original force.

cards.title: 3.2.1 Friction
body: A ball rolling along the ground gradually slows down and finally comes to rest.
A car also comes to rest once its engine is switched off.
In all these situations no force appears to be acting on the objects, yet their speed gradually decreases and they come to rest after some time.
The force responsible for changing the state of motion of objects is the force of friction.

cards.title: 3.2.2 Advantages and Disadvantages of Friction
body: Car tyres are rough, so they provide high friction and prevent the car from sliding on the road.
A matchstick is lit because of friction.
When a machine is operated, there is friction between moving parts, which causes the parts to wear down and wastes energy.

cards.title: 3.2.3 Methods of Reducing Friction
body: When surfaces are highly polished, there are fewer irregularities and friction decreases.
When oil, grease or graphite is applied between the moving parts of a machine, it forms a thin layer which prevents the moving surfaces from directly rubbing against each other.
The oil reduces the interlocking of irregularities and movement becomes smooth.
The substances which decrease friction are called **lubricants**.

cards.title: 3.2.4 Types of Friction
body: The amount of friction that exists between two bodies depends on the state of each of the bodies, that is whether they are at rest, sliding or rolling.
Depending upon these different states, friction can be classified into three types.
The frictional force present between two bodies in contact when there is no relative motion between them is called **static friction**, fs.
The force of gravity mg is cancelled by the normal reaction force, FN, of the table.

cards.title: 3.2.5 The Laws of Friction
body: Friction experiments indicate that there are certain factors that affect friction.
The magnitude of the friction force depends on the force pressing the two surfaces together and on the nature of the surfaces.
**The coefficient of friction** is a unit less quantity.
The larger the value of the coefficient of friction, the larger is the friction present between two surfaces.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following physical quantities is the quantitative measure of a body's inertia?
cards.why:
**Given:** Inertia of a body.

**Formula:** Mass is defined as the quantitative measure of a body's inertia. The larger the mass, the more the body resists changes to its state of motion.

**Substitution:** While weight changes with gravity, mass is constant and directly measures the body's resistance to acceleration.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **D. Mass**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Frictional force between two solid sliding surfaces is independent of the:

options.A: A. Normal force pressing them together
options.C: C. Nature of the materials in contact

cards.why:
**Given:** Frictional properties.

**Formula:** According to the laws of friction, $$f = \mu F_N$$.

**Substitution:** Friction depends on the coefficient of friction (material nature and roughness) and the normal force, but is independent of the apparent area of contact.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **B. Apparent area of contact**.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Friction depends on surface roughness and how hard the surfaces press together.

**Step 2:** Oil forms a thin layer that keeps the surfaces apart.

**Step 3:** Roughening, extra pressure and removing bearings increase friction.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Linear Momentum
body: A truck, which is a large mass, does not require any attention when parked.
A small mass moving with high speed, such as a bullet fired from a gun, may hurt or kill a person.
A bicycle and a motor car are moving with the same speed.
Two motor cars of equal mass are moving at different speeds.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Impulse
body: In a high jump athletic event, the athletes are made to fall on a cushioned bed.
An understanding of Newton’s second law of motion is needed to answer these questions.
Impulse should usually be considered when very large force acts for a very short period of time.
Impulse is also defined as the change in momentum.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Conservation of Momentum
body: During collision which lasts for a time ∆t, the ball A exerts a force FAB on ball B and the ball B exerts a force FBA on ball A.
The momenta (plural from of momentum) of ball A before and after the collision are mAuA and mAvA, respectively.
A bullet of mass 20 g is fired with a velocityof 150 m/s from a pistol of mass 2 kg.

cards.title: Change in momentum and average force
cards.problem: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and bounces straight back at 8 m/s. The contact time is 0.05 s. Find the change in momentum and the average force on the ball.

steps.text: Take the direction towards the wall as positive: u = +10 m/s, v = −8 m/s.
Change in momentum: Δp = m(v − u) = 0.2 × (−8 − 10) = −3.6 kg·m/s.
Average force: F = Δp ÷ t = −3.6 ÷ 0.05 = −72 N.
The minus sign means the force on the ball points away from the wall.

cards.answer: Δp = 3.6 kg·m/s away from the wall; average force = 72 N away from the wall.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. What is its momentum?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Momentum $p = mv$.

**Step 2:** $p = 2 \times 3$.

**Step 3:** $= 6$ kg·m/s.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 4 m/s has a momentum of:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Formula: p = m × v.

**Step 2:** Substitute: p = 0.5 kg × 4 m/s.

**Step 3:** Answer: p = 2 kg·m/s.

**Tip:** Momentum is a vector – it has the direction of the velocity.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A force of 20 N acts on a body for 0.3 s. The impulse given to the body is:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Formula: impulse J = F × t.

**Step 2:** Substitute: J = 20 N × 0.3 s.

**Step 3:** Answer: J = 6 N·s, which equals the change in momentum.

**Tip:** 1 N·s = 1 kg·m/s, so impulse and momentum change have the same unit.

glossary.meaning: Extension is the increase in length from the normal, unstretched length of the spring; compression is the decrease from its normal length.
Force is defined as a push or a pull on an object.
Elastic limit is the limit to the applied force from which the material will recover when the force is removed.
Inertia is a property of matter that is constant everywhere in the universe.
Mass is a measure of an object’s inertia.
Apparent weight is the force an object experiences as a result of all the forces which act on it to give the object acceleration.
Gravitational force is a property of all matter; that is, every object attracts every other object with a gravitational force.
Normal force is a contact force between two solid objects and acts that is perpendicularly to the contact surfaces (e.g. cupboard and floor).
Friction is defined as the force which opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact.
Momentum is a vector quantity and its SI unit is kg.m/s.
Impulse is a vector quantity and its SI unit is N.s or kg.m/s.

tips.text: Force is defined as a push or a pull on an object. It is a vector quantity and its SI unit is the newton (N).
Net force, resultant force or unbalanced force is the vector sum of all the forces acting on an object at the same time.
A force exerted on an object may change the shape and size of the object, change the velocity of the object, or change the direction of motion of the object.
Elastic materials are materials that recover their original shape and size when the force is removed after they are stretched, compressed, bent or twisted.
Inelastic materials are materials that do not return to their original shape when the force is removed.
Elastic limit is the limit to the applied force from which the material will recover when the force is removed.

The Italian Galileo Galilei (1564 - 1642) was one of the first scientists to understand that a force doesn’t need to be continually applied to an object to keep it moving. He claimed that no resultant force is required to maintain uniform motion.
Galileo explained that a force is needed to keep an object moving on a level surface because the force of friction opposes the motion.
Without friction, an object will never stop moving.
To prove this statement, Galileo conducted an experiment using two inclined planes set end-to-end, one tilted down and the other up. He rolled a ball down the first incline.

questions.q: State Newton's first law in one line.
questions.answer: An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a net (resultant) force acts on it.
why: Zero net force means zero acceleration.
So the velocity (speed and direction) stays constant.
A change of velocity needs a net force.
questions.label: 1. State Newton's first law in one line.
questions.tip: N1: no net force ↔ no acceleration.

similar.q: In a uniform circular motion like the orbits of the planets and the orbits of natural and communication satellites, the directions of acceleration and force are  A) towards the center of the circle.  B) away from the center of the circle.  C) tangent to the motion of the object.  D) parallel to the velocity of the object.  E) anti-parallel to the velocity of the object.
similar.a: A. towards the center of the circle. — The velocity is tangential, perpendicular to the acceleration. Answer: A.

questions.q: What is inertia?
questions.answer: The tendency of an object to resist a change in its velocity; mass measures it.
why: Objects keep doing what they are doing unless a force acts (Newton's first law).
The bigger the mass, the harder it is to start, stop or turn the object.
So mass is the measure of inertia.
questions.label: 2. What is inertia?
questions.tip: Passengers jerk forward when a bus brakes – inertia.

similar.a: D. Inertia. — Mass is the measure of inertia. Answer: D.

questions.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
questions.answer: Mass is the amount of matter (kg) and does not change; weight is the gravitational force on it (N) and depends on g.
why: Mass is a scalar measured in kilograms.
Weight W = mg is a force (vector, downward) measured in newtons.
Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes with g (e.g. on the Moon).
questions.label: 5. What is the difference between mass and weight?
questions.tip: Balance measures mass; spring balance measures weight.

questions.q: An astronaut's weight is smaller on the Moon. What happens to the mass?
questions.answer: The mass stays the same.
why: Mass is the amount of matter – it does not depend on place.
Weight W = mg; g on the Moon ≈ 1.6 N/kg, about 1/6 of Earth's.
So weight falls to about 1/6, mass is unchanged.
questions.label: 6. An astronaut's weight is smaller on the Moon. What happens to the mass?
questions.tip: Only the g in W = mg changes from place to place.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. Name the Newton's-third-law pair for the force the book exerts on the table.
questions.answer: The table pushes up on the book (normal force). The book's weight pairs with the book pulling the Earth up.
why: Third-law pairs are equal, opposite, the same type of force, and act on two different objects.
Book pushes down on table ↔ table pushes up on book (both contact forces).
Earth pulls book down (weight) ↔ book pulls Earth up (gravity).

questions.q: Why do Newton's-third-law forces not cancel each other?
questions.answer: Because they act on two different objects.
why: Forces cancel only when they act on the same object.
An action–reaction pair always acts on two different bodies.
Each force affects the motion of its own object.
questions.label: 8. Why do Newton's-third-law forces not cancel each other?
questions.tip: To see if forces cancel, look at one object only (free-body diagram).

similar.q: Two objects of different masses move with different velocities in opposite directions on a horizontal surface. When they collide, the  A) momentum of each one remains constant.  B) kinetic energy of each one remains constant.  C) total momentum of all the objects remains constant.  D) momentum of both objects equals to their total kinetic energy.  E) total kinetic energy of all objects is zero.
similar.a: C. total momentum of all the objects remains constant. — Kinetic energy may be lost (inelastic); momentum and energy have different units, so D is meaningless. Answer: C.

questions.q: An object rests on level ground. How big is the normal force?
questions.answer: Equal to its weight (if no other vertical forces act).
why: At rest, acceleration = 0, so the net vertical force = 0.
Forces: weight mg down, normal force N up.
N − mg = 0, so N = mg.

questions.answer: N = 50 N, f_max = 20 N
why: On level ground N = mg = 5 kg × 10 m/s² = 50 N.
f_max = μN = 0.4 × 50 N.

questions.q: A horizontal force of 10 N pushes the 5 kg block at rest (f_max = 20 N). Does it slide?
questions.answer: No – 10 N is less than the 20 N maximum static friction, so it stays at rest.
why: Static friction adjusts to match the push, up to f_max = 20 N.
The push is 10 N < 20 N.
So friction = 10 N, the net force is 0 and the block stays at rest.

questions.tip: The block moves only when the push exceeds f_max.

similar.q: A 20 kg block rests on a horizontal surface with coefficient of static friction of 0.5. The force needed, in newtons, to just start the block to move is [g = 10 m/s²]  A) 10.  B) 50.  C) 100.  D) 150.  E) 200.
similar.a: C. 100. — Maximum static friction fs = μs N = 0.5 × 200 = 100 N; a horizontal force just exceeding this starts the motion (G9 pp.177–181). Answer: C.

questions.q: How does kinetic friction compare with static friction?
questions.answer: Kinetic friction acts while sliding and is usually smaller than the maximum static friction.
why: Static friction acts when surfaces do not slide and can grow up to μₛN.
Once sliding starts, kinetic friction μₖN acts.
Usually μₖ < μₛ – it is easier to keep a box moving than to start it.
questions.label: 12. How does kinetic friction compare with static friction?
questions.tip: Hard to start, easier to keep going.

similar.q: Reduce friction?

questions.q: Give ways to reduce friction.
questions.answer: Smooth/polish the surfaces, lubricate (oil, grease), use wheels or ball bearings, use an air cushion.
why: Friction comes from surfaces rubbing and gripping.
Lubricants separate the surfaces; rolling replaces sliding.
Smoother surfaces and air cushions (hovercraft) reduce contact.
questions.label: 13. Give ways to reduce friction.
questions.tip: Remember "SLOW": Smooth, Lubricate, Oil/rollers, Wheels.

similar.q: Useful friction?

questions.q: Give examples where friction is useful.
questions.answer: Walking, brakes, gripping a pen, nails and screws holding, tyres on roads.
why: Friction opposes sliding between surfaces.
Without it, feet and tyres would slip and objects could not be held.
So friction is needed for walking, braking and holding things together.
questions.label: 14. Give examples where friction is useful.
questions.tip: Think of ice – everything that becomes hard on ice needs friction.

similar.q: p of 2 kg at 3 m/s?

questions.q: p of 2 kg at 3 m/s?
questions.answer: 6 kg·m/s.
why: 6 kg·m/s.
questions.label: 15. p of 2 kg at 3 m/s?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Impulse 10 N for 0.5 s?

questions.q: A force of 10 N acts for 0.5 s. What impulse does it give?
questions.answer: 5 N·s (equal to the change in momentum)
why: Impulse = F × Δt.
= 5 N·s = Δp (5 kg·m/s).
questions.label: 16. A force of 10 N acts for 0.5 s. What impulse does it give?
questions.tip: N·s and kg·m/s are the same unit.

similar.q: That Δp on 2 kg. Δv?

questions.q: That Δp on 2 kg. Δv?
questions.label: 17. That Δp on 2 kg. Δv?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Soft landing increases Δt so F?
similar.a: Smaller average F for same Δp.

questions.q: Soft landings (bending knees, mats, airbags) increase the stopping time Δt. What happens to the average force?
questions.answer: The average force becomes smaller for the same change in momentum.
why: F = Δp ÷ Δt.
The change in momentum (stopping) is fixed.
A larger Δt gives a smaller F, so less injury.
questions.label: 18. Soft landings (bending knees, mats, airbags) increase the stopping time Δt. What happens to the…
questions.tip: Longer stopping time = gentler force.

similar.q: Two skaters push. Momenta?
similar.a: Equal opposite if they start at rest (external F≈0).

questions.q: Two skaters at rest push each other apart. Compare their momenta afterwards.
questions.answer: Equal in size and opposite in direction (total still zero).
why: The total momentum before is 0 (both at rest).
External forces are negligible, so momentum is conserved.
After: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = 0, so m₁v₁ = −m₂v₂; the lighter skater moves faster.
questions.label: 19. Two skaters at rest push each other apart. Compare their momenta afterwards.
questions.tip: Explosions/push-apart from rest: momenta equal and opposite.

similar.q: 4 kg at 3 m/s hits and sticks to 2 kg at rest. v?

questions.q: A 4 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits and sticks to a 2 kg trolley at rest. What is their common velocity?
questions.answer: 2 m/s
why: Momentum is conserved: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v.
v = 2 m/s (a perfectly inelastic collision).
questions.label: 20. A 4 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits and sticks to a 2 kg trolley at rest. What is their common velocity?
questions.tip: "Stick together" = add the masses after the collision.

similar.q: g in F=GMm/r² at Earth surface ≈?

questions.q: Using F = GMm/r², what is g at the Earth's surface equal to?
questions.answer: g = GM/R² ≈ 9.8 m/s² (M = Earth's mass, R = Earth's radius)
why: The weight of a mass m is mg, and it equals the gravitational force GMm/R².
mg = GMm/R², so m cancels.
questions.label: 21. Using F = GMm/r², what is g at the Earth's surface equal to?
questions.tip: g does not depend on the falling object's mass.

similar.q: What is the first rule when drawing a free-body diagram?

questions.q: What is the first rule when drawing a free-body diagram?
questions.answer: Draw only the forces acting ON one chosen object.
why: Isolate one object.
Draw every force on it (weight, normal, friction, tension, applied) as arrows from the object.
Leave out forces that the object exerts on other things.
questions.label: 22. What is the first rule when drawing a free-body diagram?
questions.tip: Label each arrow with "by what on what".

similar.q: Newton's third law refers to "action-reaction forces". These forces always occur in pairs and  A) sometimes act on the same object.  B) always act on the same object.  C) may be at right angles.  D) never act on the same object.  E) always act at right angles.
similar.a: D. never act on the same object. — Action and reaction are equal in size, opposite in direction, along the same line, and act on DIFFERENT bodies (G9 p.157–160) – that is why they never cancel each other. Answer: D.

questions.q: A lift accelerates upward at 2 m/s². What is the apparent weight (normal force) of a 50 kg person in it? (g = 10 m/s²)
why: Newton's second law, up = +: N − mg = ma.
N = 600 N – the person feels heavier.
questions.label: 23. A lift accelerates upward at 2 m/s². What is the apparent weight (normal force) of a 50 kg person…
questions.tip: Accelerating up: N = m(g + a). Down: N = m(g − a).

similar.q:
A force of 5 N acts on a body of weight 10 N. The acceleration of the body, in m/s², is
[g = 10 m/s²]  A) 50.  B) 5.  C) 0.5.  D) 2.  E) 20.
similar.a: B. 5. — Newton's second law: a = F/m = 5 N ÷ 1 kg = 5 m/s² (G9 p.139–150). Answer: B. (C, 0.5, wrongly divides by the weight.)

questions.q: The same 50 kg person is in a lift accelerating downward at 2 m/s². What is the apparent weight?
why: Take down = +: mg − N = ma.
N = 400 N – the person feels lighter.
questions.label: 24. The same 50 kg person is in a lift accelerating downward at 2 m/s². What is the apparent weight?
questions.tip: In free fall (a = g) the apparent weight is zero.

similar.q: Resultant 0 but moving?

questions.q: Can an object be moving when the resultant force on it is zero?
questions.answer: Yes – it moves at constant velocity (Newton's first law).
why: Zero resultant force means zero acceleration.
Zero acceleration means the velocity does not change.
The velocity can be any constant value, not only zero.
questions.label: 25. Can an object be moving when the resultant force on it is zero?
questions.tip: Force changes motion; it is not needed to keep motion going.

similar.q: Units of μ?

questions.q: What are the units of the coefficient of friction μ?
questions.answer: None – μ is a ratio of two forces.
why: μ = f/N.
Both f and N are in newtons.
N ÷ N cancels, so μ has no unit.
questions.label: 26. What are the units of the coefficient of friction μ?
questions.tip: Ratios of the same quantity have no units.

similar.q: Gravity pair?
similar.a: You pull the Earth as hard as it pulls you — Earth barely accelerates.

questions.q: The Earth pulls you down with your weight. What is the third-law pair, and why doesn't the Earth move noticeably?
questions.answer: You pull the Earth up with an equal force; the Earth's huge mass makes its acceleration tiny.
why: Third law: Earth on you ↔ you on Earth, equal and opposite.
a = F/m: the force is the same but the Earth's mass is about 6×10²⁴ kg.
So the Earth's acceleration is far too small to notice.
questions.label: 27. The Earth pulls you down with your weight. What is the third-law pair, and why doesn't the Earth…
questions.tip: Equal forces do not mean equal accelerations.

similar.q: Trap: “Action cancels reaction, so nothing moves.” Why is this wrong?

questions.q: Trap: "Action cancels reaction, so nothing can move." Why is this wrong?
questions.answer: Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel.
why: Forces cancel only on the same object.
A horse pulls the cart; the cart pulls the horse – two different objects.
Whether the cart moves depends only on the forces on the cart.
questions.label: 28. Trap: "Action cancels reaction, so nothing can move." Why is this wrong?
questions.tip: Draw a separate free-body diagram for each object.

similar.q: Trap: why is it wrong to use f = μN when the block is not at the limit and not sliding?
similar.a: Static f ≤ μN, only as big as needed.

questions.q: Trap: why is it wrong to use f = μN when the block is not at the limit and not sliding?
questions.answer: Static friction is only as large as needed (f ≤ μN); μN is just the maximum.
why: Static friction balances the applied force: f = applied push while the block stays still.
It can rise only up to f_max = μN.
So f = μN only at the point of slipping (or with μₖ while sliding).
questions.label: 29. Trap: why is it wrong to use f = μN when the block is not at the limit and not sliding?
questions.tip: Not sliding? Find friction from the force balance, not from μN.

similar.q: When can you say that momentum p is conserved for a system?
similar.a: Check external forces first (friction, you pushing the floor).

questions.q: When can you say that the momentum p of a system is conserved?
questions.answer: When the net external force on the system is zero.
why: Δp = F_ext × Δt.
If F_ext = 0, then Δp = 0.
Check external forces such as friction or a push from the floor before using conservation.
questions.label: 30. When can you say that the momentum p of a system is conserved?
questions.tip: Internal forces (between the objects) never change total momentum.
